title: SRA In-House Conference 2025 — AI panel (regulator, vendor GC and legal-tech CEO)
author: SRA Deputy General Counsel (session chair; surname garbled in captions) · SRA panellist (addressed once, rendered "ashon" in captions) · Harry (General Counsel & AI Governance Officer, legal-AI vendor) · Wendy (former in-house lawyer; technology company CEO)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Deployment controls: Useful AI needs proportionate safeguards
st.an: The panel accepts the need for safeguards that preserve useful AI adoption and materially develops the proposition with concrete, proportionate governance practices—technology registers, disclosure, training and security coordination—plus task-selection criteria focused on relevant behaviour, available data and explainability. Its concern that European regulation may be premature is a caveat about regulatory design, not a rejection of deployment controls.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source accepts that generative AI fits language-intensive legal work and adds a concrete account of workflow-layer evolution: agents connecting research, synthesis, contextual retrieval and drafting across multiple steps. Its observation that in-house deployment is ahead of private practice also develops the cluster’s adoption analysis. The historical qualification about earlier rules-based systems does not undermine the cluster’s core proposition.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: The panel accepts that AI can redesign legal delivery beyond isolated task acceleration and materially develops the proposition through in-house examples of multi-step agents, repeatable outcomes, institutionalised knowledge and workflow-based delivery. It adds implementation, governance and training requirements while treating productivity, access and workforce effects as expectations rather than proven outcomes.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The panel directly supports the cluster’s core claim that legal AI is shifting from accelerating standalone tasks to executing connected, context-aware workflow steps. Its evidence is illustrative and predictive, however, and does not address autonomy distinctions, error propagation, verification bottlenecks or governance.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core framing by describing agents as coordinating research, contextualisation and drafting across a connected workflow rather than merely accelerating standalone tasks. It also supports the premise that text-heavy legal work is well suited to generative AI. However, it offers qualitative observations and forecasts, not evidence on expert workflow design, tacit-knowledge transfer, evaluation or retained human checkpoints.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The panel supports the cluster’s core proposition that automating routine junior work can remove experience through which legal expertise develops, requiring stronger learning scaffolds. It also aligns with the cluster’s qualified view that some hands-on repetition is valuable but indefinite repetition is not, and that employment effects remain uncertain. Its practical workflow examples reinforce task redistribution, though it provides no quantified evidence or developed training model.

st.t: Expert workflows: Legal context becomes product infrastructure
st.an: The panel supports the proposition that legal AI creates value through integrated, problem-specific workflows that institutionalise knowledge, connect multiple steps and apply risk-based human review. Its emphasis on repositories, guardrails, permissions and scoped deployment also supports the synthesis’s caution that these are emerging practices rather than proof of reliable autonomy or broad transformation.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI changes legal work while putting traditional expertise-development routes under pressure. It specifically recognises learning value in routine trainee work and advocates stronger learning scaffolds if that work disappears, while treating reduced lawyer numbers as unlikely rather than established.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of generative AI as predictive generation and of agents as autonomous sequences likely to become more prominent. It provides conceptual explanation and forecasting rather than empirical evidence, and it does not address the cluster’s central requirements of authoritative grounding, human verification, supervision or professional responsibility.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The panel aligns closely with the synthesis: AI is expected to change legal tasks and delivery rather than eliminate lawyers, while human expertise and reassurance remain important. It also supports buyer-side pressure as a catalyst, the need to redesign junior development when routine work is automated, and the qualified potential to address unmet legal need.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The panel closely supports the synthesis: it presents AI as selectively useful for repeatable workflows, stresses problem-led deployment, data coverage, explainability and proportionate governance, and expects human judgment to remain central in consequential matters. It also reinforces the synthesis’s concern that automating junior work may weaken professional development.

kp.k: In-house respondents see AI opportunity alongside challenge
kp.d: The chair cites the SRA's December 2024 risk report, surveying 515 solicitors including 102 in-house solicitors (both rendered as “sisters” in the captions), as finding the in-house community more likely to see legal technology and AI as an opportunity as well as a challenge. The chair also describes dedicated legal AI as increasingly accessible beyond the largest firms, with potential cost and speed benefits rather than measured outcomes.
qs: in our December 2024 report on risk in the legal profession we surveyed 515 sisters and that included 102 in-house sisters
dedicated AI for legal work  was once only accessible for the largest of firms but that's no longer the case

kp.k: Buyer adoption pressures external counsel to adopt
kp.d: Harry, speaking as a legal-AI vendor's GC, reports company growth moving from 10 to 15% annually to several 100% annually around 2020–2021, initially almost entirely from in-house teams. He attributes a shift toward private practice in the last year to clients questioning why external counsel do not use technologies already benefiting their own teams. This is a vendor-specific account, not market-wide adoption evidence.
qs: they were growing at 10 to 15% a year for years 2020 comes around 2021 and we've grown at several 100% a year every year
almost all of that has been on in-house teams and a tiny amount has been on Private Practice in the last year that's really shifted
the amount of In-House teams asking their external coun or why they are not using the same pieces of technology that they are seeing advantages with

kp.k: Agents extend automation from tasks to workflows
kp.d: Harry distinguishes research, analytical and generative AI, then describes agents as autonomous sequences spanning ticket receipt, research, contextualisation and draft preparation. He identifies this as a shift beyond accelerating isolated tasks, predicts more deployment over the next few years, and asserts that in-house deployment is already accelerating faster than private practice.
qs: an agent basically goes through all those steps rather than as most lawyers have I think typically thought of AI in the last 3 to four years just accelerating Standalone tasks
that is the big shift that is happening and I think we're going to see a lot more of that next few years

kp.k: Behavioural context can exceed available model data
kp.d: Drawing on financial-services compliance work, Wendy cautions that sophisticated AI may lack the data needed to recognise relevant behaviour and may be less explainable than rules-based systems. She reports interviews finding experienced compliance officers considered 20 elements not available to the algorithm. She applies this experience to legal adoption as a recommendation to investigate boundaries and unintended consequences rather than equating polished outputs with adequate understanding.
qs: we had really great highly accurate rules-based alert generation that Regulators love because you could explain exactly how the rule worked
they were looking for 20 different um elements represented by data that wasn't available to the AI algorithm
it's really important for us to understand right now where are the edges where's the unintended consequences of it

kp.k: Confidence affects critical scrutiny of AI outputs
kp.d: Wendy reports recent Microsoft research associating greater confidence in one's own ability and lower confidence in technology with stronger critical analysis of generated outputs. She contrasts this with juniors' higher confidence in technology and lower confidence in themselves, warning of implications for developing critical thinking. The transcript supplies no study sample, methods or quantified effect.
qs: if you have high confidence your own ability slightly less confidence in the technology your critical thinking of what gets produced is higher
whereas Junior people actually much higher confidence in the tech lower confidence in themselves much lower critical analysis of it

kp.k: Institutionalised knowledge supports speed and continuity
kp.d: Harry identifies repeatable, consistent use of institutional knowledge as a principal benefit of generative AI. His examples include repository-based RFP answers with higher-risk items flagged for secondary review, draft meeting minutes for human review, and smoother handovers through maintained playbooks or tracking. He illustrates potential contract-processing savings from 20–30 hours weekly to five, without identifying a measured customer study.
qs: having consistency of approach not losing institutional knowledge
automate a lot of those answers flag which ones are the highest risk that needs secondary review and the rest we're happy to generate from repository
we know that typically that takes us 20 30 hours a week and now that's taking us five hours a week

kp.k: In-house lawyers face dual adoption and governance responsibilities
kp.d: Harry argues that in-house lawyers must both improve their own practice and understand technologies used throughout the business well enough to enable safe deployment. He criticises shutting down unsanctioned use instead of providing guardrails. Wendy connects shadow IT to staff trying to complete work under pressure with inadequate tools, making actual working behaviour central to governance.
qs: one is what can we use tools to to make our own practice more efficient and what are the tools and practices that the wider business wants to use that we need to understand and guard rail
lawyers in house are increasingly Under Pressure to  understand the technologies that their wider business stakeholders are using in order to maximize them safely

people are using Tech because you know going to that point earlier about ethics and what really happens in organizations you know why do good people do bad things it's usy because they're trying to get a good job done

kp.k: Capturing tacit expertise could support junior development
kp.d: Wendy describes her company's attempt to combine behavioural interviewing and generative AI to elicit experienced professionals' contextual know-how for colleagues and juniors. She argues that hybrid work, reluctance to ask questions and departing staff make such knowledge harder to access. Her estimate that roughly 90% of knowledge remains unwritten is asserted without supporting study details; the proposed technology is presented as work underway and potential, not established training effectiveness.
qs: there's something like 90 % of what we have in our heads never gets written down
the latest geni is what we're using to train to try to pull out some of that experiential knowhow
it's really difficult to ask you know those cheapy questions it's quite difficult to go and ask a really busy person and it's even more difficult when they're not sat next to you anymore

kp.k: Adoption should start with problems and small pilots
kp.d: The SRA panellist reports that questions have shifted from why to use AI toward how to use it responsibly and compare providers. Drawing on engagement and recently concluded law-firm research, without methodological details, the panellist recommends defining the problem, starting with quick wins, consulting peers, testing software widely and negotiating suitable contract lengths. Wendy also points to collaborative capability benchmarking, with the report name unclear in the captions, as a procurement aid rather than presenting any benchmark findings.
qs: the conversation is very much shifted from why why would I use AI or Tech generally to how
defining your problem as best you can um and kind of going from that is important
pilot the software test it test it widely
opt for contract links that make sense for you and your needs

kp.k: Governance combines inventories, intake controls and legal due diligence
kp.d: Harry describes technology registers, security-team collaboration, transparent disclosure, training and simplified intake forms, including automated approval of familiar licence terms. He recommends proportional controls and leadership support, arguing that existing legal frameworks cover many issues. Wendy emphasises privilege, confidentiality, access restrictions, data protection and whether models train on customer data. These are operational recommendations, not new professional rules announced by the SRA.
qs: we have very clear full Tech stack registers not just AI
undisclosed usage is actually a much greater risk in any event
where does  our IP go who owns the output where's what are the data transfer requirements
there will be models that are training on data and those are questions that you need to ask

kp.k: AI governance is distinct from general counsel work
kp.d: Harry rejects the suggestion that GC and AI governance officer necessarily become a combined future role. He describes his own combination as contingent on interest and privacy-law experience, reports a growing separate governance profession, and argues governance includes ethical considerations beyond legal risk. He predicts greater investment in distinct roles and possible lawyer transitions into them.
qs: they're completely separate
what is necessarily the legal risk is not necessarily always the same as what is the governance risk
best practice and governance I would actually say uh includes a broader ethical consideration
you may see many lawyers transition into that role more fulltime

kp.k: Automating junior tasks risks removing formative learning
kp.d: Wendy argues that apparently menial work, such as proofreading contracts, embeds understanding of contract structure and interactions. She recommends identifying the learning lost through automation and creating scaffolds that expose juniors to nuanced variants and contextual judgment, rather than assuming repetition alone develops expertise. She also questions whether AI summaries leave lawyers sufficiently familiar with underlying documents for client discussions.
qs: what you don't realize we were doing is  learning the anatomy of a contract and what interacts with what
does experience really and expertise really developed when you see lots of nuance versions and you start to get challenged
what's the value in it that you've lost and being really careful about that
how does it work when you go and sit down in front of a client if you haven't read it first and got the knowledge in your head as well

kp.k: Human judgment may complement expanded access to legal help
kp.d: The SRA panellist expresses optimism that AI could inform consumers, equalise solicitor-client relationships and free lawyers for human-facing work that helps meet unmet legal need. The panellist expects changed work rather than fewer lawyers, explicitly as a personal view. Wendy similarly expects a continuing human role because interpretation, client goals, context and consequential decisions remain difficult for technology to capture. These are qualified expectations, not demonstrated access-to-justice or employment outcomes.
qs: the potential for AI to help consumers be more informed about their legal issues
different but not less lawyers
this huge kind of amount of unmet legal need that we know exists is actually going to start being met because lawyers will be able to do more of the kind of face-to-face human contact
ultimately people will be making judgments on what the meaning of  something is

kp.k: Regulatory convergence prediction draws on privacy history
kp.d: Harry personally characterises European AI regulation as good but somewhat premature and reports US companies saying its risk-reward balance discourages business there. By analogy with early personal-data misuse and subsequent privacy regulation, he predicts that over a 20–30-year horizon AI rules will concentrate enforcement on the greatest risks and worst offenders, with much remaining weakly enforced. This is his explicitly strong speculative view, not the SRA's regulatory position.
qs: AI regulation in Europe is good but uh slightly premature
the answer is great we just simply won't do business there
especially if we're talking over a 20 30y year uh window
a lot of it will be there in principle but not really enforced as we currently see every day with data privacy regulation

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The SRA session chair says legal AI is becoming accessible beyond the largest firms and could bring cost, speed and efficiency benefits.
pts.d: The chair describes an existing expansion in commercial products available to smaller firms and tools accessible online to anyone. The prospective benefit is more efficient legal work through removal of repetitive manual tasks, with further opportunities potentially varying by practice area. The chair cites the SRA's December 2024 risk survey of 515 solicitors, including 102 in-house solicitors, as evidence of perceptions of opportunity and challenge, not as a measurement of productivity gains.

pts.k: Harry says in-house teams led adoption at his legal-AI vendor, with their demands subsequently accelerating uptake by external counsel.
pts.d: Harry, speaking as the vendor's GC and AI Governance Officer, reports that annual company growth increased from 10–15% to several hundred percent around 2020–2021. He says most growth initially came from in-house teams and little from private practice, but that this shifted in the year preceding the 2025 panel because in-house clients were asking external counsel why they were not using equivalent technology. This is a company-specific account and Harry's explanation of its drivers, not an independently measured legal-market adoption rate.

pts.k: Harry predicts a shift from accelerating individual legal tasks to agents executing multi-step workflows.
pts.d: Harry describes agents as autonomous sequences that can process an incoming legal ticket, research an answer, consolidate it into an email, incorporate recipient context and prepare a draft. He characterises this as an existing shift that will become more prominent over the next few years, including the next two to three years. The example ends with draft preparation; it does not explicitly claim that final advice will be issued without human review. No agent performance benchmark or measured deployment result is supplied.

pts.k: Harry says generative AI can preserve institutional knowledge, standardise responses and reduce legal bottlenecks.
pts.d: Drawing on his own work and customer experience, Harry identifies repeatable outputs and institutional knowledge retention as major benefits. His examples include generating routine RFP answers from a repository while referring high-risk answers for secondary review; drafting board minutes for human review; and keeping playbooks or tracked information current so that staff departures produce smoother handovers. These combine augmentation with selective automation: the claim is not that all legal review disappears. Harry qualifies usefulness by organisation size, practice area and the ability to train repeatable outcomes.

pts.k: Harry says automation of basic contracts can release in-house capacity for more proactive, higher-value work.
pts.d: Harry offers an illustrative reduction in routine contracting workload from 20–30 hours per week to five hours. He links that released time to work the business values more and to moving beyond reactive firefighting. Although presented in a discussion of customer benefits, the transcript does not identify a customer, sample, measurement method or study behind these figures; they should be retained as his illustrative account, not a general productivity estimate.

pts.k: Harry and Wendy describe AI adoption as creating both a productivity opportunity and a wider governance burden for in-house legal teams.
pts.d: Harry distinguishes improving the legal team's own work from understanding and governing tools used throughout the business, calling the second task more complex. He says pressure on in-house lawyers to understand other business functions' technology is increasing. Wendy describes a growing shadow-IT culture in which staff under pressure bypass inconvenient approved tools to get work done. Harry argues that undisclosed use is a greater risk and favours enabling sanctioned use with guardrails over blanket shutdowns. Their support consists of operational experience and behavioural observations, rather than quantified incidence or risk data.

pts.k: The SRA panellist says the adoption problem has shifted from whether to use AI to how to select and use it responsibly.
pts.d: The SRA panellist reports that tool availability is now less of a concern than navigating providers and comparing products. This affects sole practitioners, small and large firms, and in-house teams. The speaker draws on regulatory engagement and recently concluded law-firm research, including experiences of tools failing to deliver expected benefits because they did not fit the underlying problem. Wendy adds that collaborative benchmarking can help buyers identify suitable technology, referring to a report rendered as the 'vows report' in the captions; no benchmark results or scores are provided.

pts.k: Wendy says reliance on generative AI can weaken critical analysis, particularly where users trust the technology more than their own expertise.
pts.d: Wendy invokes recent Microsoft research on generative AI and critical thinking. As she describes it, experienced people with greater confidence in themselves and less confidence in the technology analyse outputs more critically, whereas junior people with the opposite confidence pattern show less critical analysis. She connects this to the need to develop junior lawyers' critical thinking. The transcript supplies no study title, sample, quantitative effect or legal-profession-specific findings; the experience and junior-person distinctions are Wendy's account of the research.

pts.k: Wendy warns that automating routine legal work may remove learning opportunities, while suggesting AI could help transfer experienced lawyers' tacit know-how.
pts.d: Wendy uses her own trainee contract-proofreading experience to explain that apparently menial work teaches contract structure and interactions. She argues that expertise also requires exposure to nuanced cases, client conversations and unexpected developments; merely receiving an AI summary may not give a lawyer the internalised knowledge needed for a client meeting. She describes her company's developing use of generative AI and behavioural-science interviewing to elicit experienced practitioners' know-how and make it available to colleagues and juniors, particularly in hybrid working. This is a proposed training response and an ongoing development effort, not a demonstrated replacement for apprenticeship.

pts.k: Harry predicts growth in a distinct AI-governance profession rather than permanent merger of AI governance with the GC role.
pts.d: Harry explicitly separates his two current roles. He reports a booming market for standalone AI-governance professionals and predicts investment in these functions, separate AI regulators, and possible transitions by lawyers into full-time governance roles. His rationale is that governance encompasses broader ethical and industry-norm questions than legal risk alone. He says lawyers are currently well placed because existing governance frameworks draw on GDPR and related legal expertise, but gives no employment figures or fixed timetable for the predicted separation.

pts.k: The SRA panellist predicts changed rather than reduced lawyer employment, better-informed consumers and a possible reduction in unmet legal need.
pts.d: The SRA panellist says legal work is already changing and expects consumer expectations to reinforce that change. They suggest AI could give consumers a clearer understanding of legal issues and options, making their relationship with solicitors more equal. They predict continuing demand for human expertise and no reduction in lawyer numbers, expressly framing this as a personal view. They also express optimism, rather than a demonstrated finding, that automation could release lawyers for face-to-face work and help meet currently unmet legal need. The cited engagement and research concern people's desire for human contact, not a quantified employment or access-to-justice forecast.

pts.k: Wendy predicts a sustained human role in legal interpretation, contextual judgment and guiding clients through consequential decisions.
pts.d: Wendy says technology can help explore different ways of looking at an issue, but people will continue to judge meaning and determine how to proceed. She argues that technology remains some way from capturing all the organisational context, participants' objectives and practical constraints needed to reach an appropriate outcome. Her forecast is a continuing interaction between technology and humans for 'quite a long time', not a specified date or a claim that all current tasks remain human. It draws on her in-house and behavioural-science experience.

pts.k: Harry predicts that AI regulation will eventually concentrate in practice on the greatest risks and worst offenders, and says current European rules can deter market entry.
pts.d: This is a broader AI-market and governance claim relevant to in-house advisers. Harry calls European regulation good but somewhat premature, reporting that US companies tell him the risk–reward balance currently discourages doing business there. Drawing an analogy with the development of personal-data regulation, he predicts that over a 20–30-year horizon AI regulation across jurisdictions will focus enforcement on the greatest harms, with much remaining regulation present in principle but not heavily enforced. This is explicitly his view, supported by conversations and historical analogy rather than enforcement data or an identified company sample.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The panel combines survey findings, research references, professional experience and explicitly personal forecasts; it supplies few independently documented outcome measures.
pts.d: The chair's December 2024 SRA survey concerns perceived opportunities and risks. The SRA panellist also references newly concluded law-firm research and regulatory engagement without giving detailed methods or results. Harry's growth figures are a vendor insider's account, and his time-saving example lacks a named case or measurement protocol. Wendy references Microsoft critical-thinking research, behavioural-science methods and practitioner interviews; her estimate that around 90% of knowledge is unwritten is not sourced in the transcript. Benchmarking is discussed as a procurement aid, but no scores are reported. Predictions about headcount, access to justice, distinct governance careers and long-term enforcement are not accompanied by forecasting models.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most operational claims concern current practice in 2025; agents are a near-term forecast, while training, employment and regulatory changes have less definite or longer horizons.
pts.d: Harry dates the vendor's acceleration to around 2020–2021 and the shift toward private-practice demand to the preceding year. He anticipates more agent-based workflows over the next few years. The audience raises a 10-, 20- and 30-year training question, but the panellists do not commit to a dated workforce forecast. Harry expressly uses a 20–30-year horizon for regulatory development, despite being asked about the next one to two years. Benefits are repeatedly conditional on fit with a defined problem, organisation size, practice area, repeatability, appropriate governance and human review where needed. Wendy's tacit-knowledge capture is still being developed, and the access-to-justice outcome is framed as a possibility.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed changes affect in-house buyers, external firms, junior and experienced practitioners, emerging governance specialists, and consumers with unmet legal needs.
pts.d: In-house teams are described as early adopters, purchasers influencing external counsel, and governors of organisation-wide use. Private-practice firms face client pressure to adopt, while smaller firms gain access to products previously associated with large firms. Junior lawyers may lose routine learning opportunities and need new developmental support; experienced lawyers provide judgment, review and tacit knowledge that technology may help distribute. AI-governance roles may become distinct career paths, including for lawyers. Businesses may benefit from faster routine legal processing and fewer handover disruptions. Consumers may become better informed, and people with unmet civil legal needs could benefit if released lawyer capacity is directed toward human-facing legal help. These consumer outcomes are distinct from enterprise efficiency savings.
